items.officialTitle: Authorizes bonds for housing affordability programs
items.plainEnglish: Lets the state borrow $11.25 billion. $10 billion goes to existing affordable housing programs, including about $7.2 billion for rental housing, and $1.25 billion to CalVet home loans for veterans.
items.why: Placed on the ballot by the California Legislature. The official arguments below explain each side's stated goals.
items.yes: The state could borrow $11.25 billion to support veterans and affordable housing. LAO estimates up to 40,000 subsidized rentals and up to 40,000 households helped to buy.
items.no: The state could not borrow this money for veterans and affordable housing.
items.benefits: Up to about 40,000 subsidized rentals and 40,000 assisted home buyers (LAO estimate, not a requirement).
items.risks: Decades of fixed debt with no guaranteed number of homes. Trade-off. More subsidized homes now, in exchange for about $500 million to $600 million a year in repayments for about 25 years.
items.affected: Low and moderate income renters and buyers, veterans, farmworkers, tribes, UC and CSU students.
items.fiscal: LAO estimates taxpayers repay about $500 million to $600 million a year for about 25 years. Veterans repay the $1.25 billion CalVet share through their loans.
items.evidence: Accountability. An annual public report on the bond's investments, using the existing state housing annual report (Health and Safety Code Section 50408). A yearly independent accountant review of CalVet's home loan finances. No target for homes built or cost per home. Ratings on seven evidence factors, with reasons and sources, are in the full proposition tool.
items.uncertain: Cost per home and how fast the money gets spent.
items.argFor: Supporters' official argument says it builds affordable homes for veterans, seniors and working families with accountability and no new taxes.
items.argAgainst: No official argument against was filed. In news reports, critics such as state Sen. Tony Strickland say the state should not take on more debt.
items.supporters: Self-Help for the Elderly, California Federation of Teachers, US Vets (official argument). Gov. Newsom signed the bill placing it on the ballot.
items.opponents: No official argument against was filed. News reports name Sen. Tony Strickland as a critic. No organized campaign against.
items.notes: Every field was audited on 2026-10-22 against the official voter guide, the LAO analysis, the official arguments and, where it could be read, the legal text, by automated research. A log of the corrections is kept with the guide's records. No person has reviewed the result, so it is not marked Verified.
gaps: Which agency publishes the annual report under Section 54088 (the measure does not name it)
Whether the CalVet accountant review is made public; the text sends it only to named officials and committees

items.plainEnglish: Raises the rainy day fund's limit for required deposits from 10% to 20% of General Fund taxes, saves extra in big capital gains years, counts deposits against the state spending limit only when the money is withdrawn, and extends extra pension and retiree health debt payments from 2030 to 2040.
items.why: Placed on the ballot by the California Legislature. The official arguments below explain each side's stated goals.
items.yes: Rules for building state budget reserves and paying down extra state debts would change. LAO says state budget reserves would be higher, with more saved in the rainy day fund in certain years. The state also would be required to make extra debt payments for longer, through 2040 instead of 2030.
items.no: Rules for building state budget reserves and paying down extra state debts would not change.
items.benefits: Larger reserves built in good years, plus extra debt payments through 2040.
items.risks: Lawmakers can still suspend deposits or withdraw money in a budget emergency. Trade-off. A bigger cushion for recessions, in exchange for less money to spend on programs or rebates in years when more is saved.
items.affected: The state budget, people who use state services, schools, taxpayers.
items.fiscal: No new tax or program. It shifts when money is spent: higher reserves, and extra debt payments required through 2040 instead of 2030. LAO gives no dollar estimate or timeline for reaching 20%.
items.evidence: Accountability. No new audit or evaluator. The Department of Finance must report deposit estimates to the Legislature and each budget must include them. Deposits can still be suspended only in a budget emergency. Ratings on seven evidence factors, with reasons and sources, are in the full proposition tool.
items.uncertain: How many years it would take to actually reach 20%.
items.argFor: Supporters' official argument says doubling the reserve cap protects schools, health care and public safety in downturns.
items.argAgainst: Opponents' official argument calls it a slush fund that weakens the spending limit and makes taxpayer rebates less likely.
items.supporters: California Professional Firefighters, Assembly Budget Chair Jesse Gabriel, Los Angeles Area Chamber of Commerce (official argument). The official guide also lists Gov. Newsom.
items.opponents: David Tangipa (Assembly Budget Committee vice chair), Steven Choi (Senate Elections and Constitutional Amendments Committee vice chair) and Carl DeMaio (Reform California), official argument.
items.notes: Every field was audited on 2026-10-22 against the official voter guide, the LAO analysis, the official arguments and, where it could be read, the legal text, by automated research. A log of the corrections is kept with the guide's records. No person has reviewed the result, so it is not marked Verified.
gaps: Whether the amendment to Article XVI, Section 22 changes how a budget emergency is declared or limits withdrawals
Which Department of Finance reporting duties are new and which already exist
Recent rainy day fund suspensions and withdrawal amounts, from an official budget source

items.officialTitle: Provides permanent funding for schools and health care by extending existing tax on high incomes
items.plainEnglish: Makes permanent the higher income tax rates on income over about $371,000 for single filers, adjusted yearly for inflation. The rates now apply through 2030 and are set to expire in 2031. Rates themselves do not change.
items.why: Placed on the ballot by citizen petition (initiative). The official arguments below explain each side's stated goals.
items.yes: An income tax increase on high-income earners in place since 2012 would become permanent instead of expiring in 2031. LAO estimates $5 billion to $15 billion a year from 2031 on, roughly 40% for schools and community colleges.
items.no: The tax increase on high-income earners would expire in 2031. Those rates on about the top 2% of filers would drop back.
items.benefits: Continued funding for schools and health care after 2030.
items.risks: The budget keeps leaning on a small group of earners whose income swings with markets. Trade-off. Steady school and health funding, in exchange for keeping higher rates on top earners permanently.
items.affected: About the top 2% of filers, public schools and community colleges, and other state programs including health care.
items.fiscal: LAO estimates the rates keep $5 billion to $15 billion a year in state revenue. They apply only to income above about $371,000 for single filers, adjusted for inflation. No official per-filer example was found.
items.evidence: Accountability. Schools and colleges must post yearly accountings of this money online, their existing annual independent audits must check it, and the Controller audits the account. No student or health outcome target. Ratings on seven evidence factors, with reasons and sources, are in the full proposition tool.
items.uncertain: Whether high earners move or shift income over the long run.
items.argFor: Supporters' official argument says it keeps current rates on the top 2% to fund schools and health care, with annual independent audits.
items.argAgainst: Opponents' official argument says it makes a temporary tax permanent and the state should fix wasteful spending first.
items.supporters: California Teachers Association, California School Nurses Organization, Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California (official argument), California State PTA.
items.opponents: California Taxpayers Association, Family Business Association of California, California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce (official argument), Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association (rebuttal).
items.notes: Every field was audited on 2026-10-22 against the official voter guide, the LAO analysis, the official arguments and, where it could be read, the legal text, by automated research. A log of the corrections is kept with the guide's records. No person has reviewed the result, so it is not marked Verified.
gaps: Number of rate brackets, from LAO Figure 1 or the Franchise Tax Board rate schedule (thresholds confirmed in the official summary: about $371,000 single, $742,000 joint, $505,000 head of household, 2025 levels)
Whether the online posting, audit and Controller duties are carried over from Prop 30 or are new

items.officialTitle: Repeals prohibition against public funding of election campaigns
items.plainEnglish: Repeals the state ban on public funding of campaigns, so governments may create voluntary public funding programs for candidates. It creates no program by itself and raises the top fine for foreign campaign contributions to three times the amount.
items.why: Placed on the ballot by the California Legislature. The official arguments below explain each side's stated goals.
items.yes: State and local governments could create public campaign financing programs, with limits on which funds are used, how, and who receives them. Programs cannot favor candidates by party or incumbency. Candidates must show broad support and accept spending limits.
items.no: The state and most local governments would remain unable to create public campaign financing programs. Certain charter cities keep their existing exemption.
items.benefits: Some governments may choose to create public financing programs for candidates.
items.risks: Opponents say there is no limit on how many candidates get public money or how much. LAO says program costs could be significant for governments that create them. Trade-off. A path for candidates without wealthy backers, in exchange for public money spent on campaigns at costs set later.
items.affected: Candidates, state and local governments, taxpayers where programs are adopted.
items.fiscal: LAO estimates state costs of a few hundred thousand dollars a year. Any program's cost is set later by the government that adopts it.
items.evidence: Accountability. Existing campaign disclosure rules apply. No new audit or outcome target. The state ethics commission is not required to enforce local programs. Ratings on seven evidence factors, with reasons and sources, are in the full proposition tool.
items.uncertain: Which governments adopt programs, and at what cost.
items.argFor: Supporters' official argument says elections should be won, not bought, and this lets communities choose public financing, with safeguards. Their rebuttal says California is the only state that bans it.
items.argAgainst: Opponents' official argument says it lets politicians spend taxpayer money on campaigns with no cap on recipients or amounts.
items.supporters: League of Women Voters of California, California Nurses Association, Sen. Tom Umberg, California Common Cause.
items.opponents: California Taxpayers Association, Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, former FPPC chair Dan Schnur.
items.notes: Every field was audited on 2026-10-22 against the official voter guide, the LAO analysis, the official arguments and, where it could be read, the legal text, by automated research. A log of the corrections is kept with the guide's records. No person has reviewed the result, so it is not marked Verified.
gaps: Whether the measure caps total public money a local program may spend

items.officialTitle: Changes recall election process for statewide officers
items.plainEnglish: Recall ballots for state officers ask only whether to remove the official. If a governor is recalled, the Lieutenant Governor becomes governor. If the recall happens in the first two years of the term, before the next statewide nomination period closes, the Lieutenant Governor serves until voters elect a new governor at a future statewide election. Other recalled offices are filled under existing rules, usually a special election for legislators and a governor's appointment for other statewide offices.
items.why: Placed on the ballot by the California Legislature. The official arguments below explain each side's stated goals.
items.yes: Recall elections would no longer include a question about who should fill the vacancy. Vacancies would be filled through special elections or appointments, depending on the office and timing.
items.no: Voters would continue to be asked who should fill the vacancy as part of recall elections. In 2003 there were 135 replacement candidates on the ballot, and the winner needed only the most votes.
items.benefits: Recalled officials are replaced by succession, special election or appointment instead of a same-ballot plurality vote.
items.risks: Voters lose a direct say in the replacement, and later in a term the successor serves without a new election. Trade-off. Avoiding replacements chosen by a small plurality, in exchange for voters no longer picking the successor on the recall ballot.
items.affected: The governor and other state officers, voters in recall elections.
items.fiscal: LAO says the net fiscal effect is unknown, could be savings or costs, and is under 0.1% of the General Fund.
items.evidence: Accountability. No new audit or reporting requirement was found in the official materials. Ratings on seven evidence factors, with reasons and sources, are in the full proposition tool.
items.uncertain: How often recalls will happen in future.
items.argFor: Supporters' official argument says a replacement should not take office with a small fraction of the vote, and recalls should not be used to redo an election.
items.argAgainst: Opponents' official argument says it takes away voters' power to pick a replacement and hands the choice to Sacramento insiders.
items.supporters: League of Women Voters of California, California Common Cause, former FPPC chair Dan Schnur.
items.opponents: Senate Minority Leader Brian Jones and Assemblymember Joe Patterson (official argument). CalMatters reports almost all legislative Republicans also opposed it.
items.notes: Every field was audited on 2026-10-22 against the official voter guide, the LAO analysis, the official arguments and, where it could be read, the legal text, by automated research. A log of the corrections is kept with the guide's records. No person has reviewed the result, so it is not marked Verified.
gaps: Whether the measure adds any reporting or audit duty (none found so far)

items.officialTitle: Creates loan program for middle-income buyers of qualified new homes
items.plainEnglish: Lets the state housing finance agency (CalHFA) sell up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to lend buyers earning up to 200% of area median income up to 17% of a new home's price. Homes must be priced below about $1 million to $1.5 million depending on county, and buyers must have lived in California for one year and live in the home. The buyer puts at least 3% down. Builders who opt into higher labor standards also get different construction defect lawsuit rules.
items.why: Placed on the ballot by citizen petition (initiative). The official arguments below explain each side's stated goals.
items.yes: The state would create a new homebuying assistance program funded by up to $25 billion in revenue bonds, repaid by homeowners' loan payments.
items.no: The state would not be required to create a new homebuying assistance program. CalHFA's existing down payment programs continue.
items.benefits: More middle-income households able to buy newly built homes with 3% down.
items.risks: Buyers carry a second loan of up to 17% of the price. More buying power could also push new-home prices up, a risk no official analysis addresses. Trade-off. Easier entry to homeownership for some buyers, in exchange for more household debt and possible upward pressure on new-home prices.
items.affected: Middle-income households buying newly built homes, home builders.
items.fiscal: LAO finds no direct state or local cost, and the bonds are repaid by homeowners, not the state. On an $800,000 home a buyer would put at least $24,000 down and could borrow up to $136,000 from the program (this tool's example, using the 3% minimum and 17% maximum).
items.evidence: Accountability. The measure requires an independent annual audit of the program to confirm bond money is used as the law requires. Program rules are exempt from the state's normal rulemaking process, though CalHFA's board must approve them. No target for homes or loans. Ratings on seven evidence factors, with reasons and sources, are in the full proposition tool.
items.uncertain: The fixed interest rate CalHFA will set on the state loan, and how many people use it.
items.argFor: Supporters' official argument says private bond investors fund the loans, so taxpayers pay nothing and take no risk.
items.argAgainst: No official argument against was filed. CalMatters lists Reform California and the League of Women Voters as opponents.
items.supporters: California Conference of Carpenters, Fiona Ma (CalHFA board), California State Commanders Veterans Council (official argument). The official guide also lists United Nurses Associations of California. CalMatters also lists the California Association of Realtors.
items.opponents: No official argument against was filed. CalMatters lists Reform California and the League of Women Voters.
items.notes: Every field was audited on 2026-10-22 against the official voter guide, the LAO analysis, the official arguments and, where it could be read, the legal text, by automated research. A log of the corrections is kept with the guide's records. No person has reviewed the result, so it is not marked Verified.
gaps: Income limit wording: the official summary says 'less than twice' area median income, an earlier LAO letter says 'no more than 200 percent'
Evidence on how the program would affect home prices and how many renters it would help (no official analysis found)

items.officialTitle: Authorizes bonds for immunology medical research
items.plainEnglish: Borrows $8.4 billion for immunology research. About half goes to one institute picked by the state health department, and the rest to grants through a council of UC campuses and other California institutions. At least $4.2 billion must target cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer's.
items.why: Placed on the ballot by citizen petition (initiative). The official arguments below explain each side's stated goals.
items.yes: The state could borrow $8.4 billion to support immunology and immunotherapy research by California institutes and universities.
items.no: The state could not borrow $8.4 billion for this research.
items.benefits: Immunology research funded at one institute and through competitive grants.
items.risks: CalMatters reports the criteria for half the money likely fit one institute whose board the sponsor chairs. The campaign disputes this. Trade-off. Steady research funding, in exchange for about $500 million to $600 million a year in repayments for benefits that may take decades.
items.affected: Taxpayers, researchers, one UC-affiliated institute, patients.
items.fiscal: LAO estimates taxpayers repay $500 million to $600 million a year for about 20 years. Funded researchers must pay the state 10% of revenue from licensing or selling their discoveries, which goes to the General Fund until the bond costs are covered. LAO says this could offset part or all of the cost, but it is uncertain and could take decades.
items.evidence: Accountability. Annual public reports, including progress toward research goals, and independent financial audits for the institute and the grant council. The health department reviews the institute's agreement every five years. No numeric research targets. Ratings on seven evidence factors, with reasons and sources, are in the full proposition tool.
items.uncertain: Whether the research pays off, scientifically or financially.
items.argFor: Supporters' official argument says it speeds cures, offsets federal research cuts, and requires a 20% patient discount and audits.
items.argAgainst: Opponents' official argument says borrowing is the wrong way to fund research, the benefits rarely flow back to the state treasury, and ballot measures should not steer research toward chosen topics.
items.supporters: Sponsor Gary Michelson. The official argument is signed by leaders of Alzheimer's Los Angeles, the ALS Association and the Kidney Cancer Association.
items.opponents: Robert M. Kaplan (official argument). CalMatters also lists the League of Women Voters and several newspaper editorial boards.
items.notes: Every field was audited on 2026-10-22 against the official voter guide, the LAO analysis, the official arguments and, where it could be read, the legal text, by automated research. A log of the corrections is kept with the guide's records. No person has reviewed the result, so it is not marked Verified.
gaps: Editorial board opponents were read once only, from CalMatters

items.officialTitle: Prohibits citizens from voting unless they present government-issued identification
items.plainEnglish: Requires government ID to vote in person and the last four digits of an ID number on mail ballots. The state must offer a free voter ID card, make best efforts to verify voters' citizenship, and report results yearly.
items.why: Placed on the ballot by citizen petition (initiative). The official arguments below explain each side's stated goals.
items.yes: Voters would be required to present additional identifying information to elections officials each time they vote.
items.no: A voter's identity would continue to be established with the voter's signature.
items.benefits: Every counted ballot tied to a government ID, with yearly public reports of the share of each county's voters whose citizenship is verified.
items.risks: The official summary says mail ballots without matching ID digits would not count, and the measure sets no notice or fix-it process. Opponents say valid ballots could be thrown out. Trade-off. A uniform ID rule and public citizenship reporting, in exchange for added costs and the risk that some valid mail ballots are rejected.
items.affected: All voters, including about 13 million who voted by mail in 2024, and county election offices.
items.fiscal: LAO estimates added state and local costs of tens of millions to low hundreds of millions of dollars a year.
items.evidence: Accountability. The State Auditor audits the state and every county in odd-numbered years, counties report citizenship-verified shares yearly, and citizens may sue. No penalties or numeric targets. Ratings on seven evidence factors, with reasons and sources, are in the full proposition tool.
items.uncertain: How existing voters add an ID number, and how many ballots get rejected.
items.argFor: Supporters' official argument says bipartisan voter ID builds trust, keeps mail voting, offers a free ID and adds citizenship checks.
items.argAgainst: Opponents' official argument says it adds costly barriers and could reject ballots from seniors, students and people who changed names.
items.supporters: Californians for Voter ID (official argument). The Transparency Foundation, California Women's Leadership Association and Latino American Political Association (official rebuttal). The official guide also lists the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association. LAist also lists the California Republican Party.
items.opponents: ACLU California Action, Common Cause, League of Women Voters of California (official argument).

sources.label: Cantoni and Pons study of strict ID laws (NBER)

items.officialTitle: Imposes one-time tax on certain taxpayers
items.plainEnglish: Taxes people worth $1 billion or more who lived in California on January 1, 2026 at 5% of their net worth, once, with a lower rate just above $1 billion. It can be paid over five years with a 7.5% yearly charge on the unpaid balance. Real estate, pensions and retirement accounts are generally excluded. After administrative costs, 90% goes to public health care and 10% to education and food assistance.
items.why: Placed on the ballot by citizen petition (initiative). The official arguments below explain each side's stated goals.
items.yes: The state would collect a one-time tax from billionaires equal to 5 percent of their wealth. LAO estimates tens of billions of dollars over several years.
items.no: The state would not collect this one-time tax.
items.benefits: A one-time transfer of tens of billions from billionaires to public health care over about five years.
items.risks: Court challenges are likely. LAO's analysis of Prop 40 says that if Prop 41 or 42 gets more yes votes, courts could find a conflict and Prop 40 could be stopped even if a majority votes yes. Trade-off. Tens of billions for health care, in exchange for legal uncertainty and possible long-term income tax losses if billionaires leave.
items.affected: A few hundred billionaires according to LAO (the supporters' argument says about 200), and public health care programs.
items.fiscal: LAO says tens of billions over several years. Hoover estimates about $40 billion and supporters about $100 billion. LAO also notes the state could lose under $1 billion a year in income tax if billionaires leave.
items.evidence: Accountability. A yearly Department of Finance report to the Legislature, Franchise Tax Board review of every return, understatement penalties, and a fast court validation case. No State Auditor audit of the spending. Ratings on seven evidence factors, with reasons and sources, are in the full proposition tool.
items.uncertain: How courts treat the look-back residency date.
items.argFor: Supporters' official argument says federal cuts took health coverage away and a one-time tax on billionaires would restore it.
items.argAgainst: Opponents' official argument says it is a risky tax that would drive out residents and businesses and has no spending safeguards.
items.supporters: SEIU-UHW (official argument and rebuttal). The official guide also lists U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders as a supporter.
items.opponents: California Medical Association, California Primary Care Association, California School Boards Association (official argument). Independent reports add Gov. Newsom. A committee funded largely by Sergey Brin backs Props 41 and 42 and opposes Prop 40.
items.notes: Every field was audited on 2026-10-22 against the official voter guide, the LAO analysis, the official arguments and, where it could be read, the legal text, by automated research. A log of the corrections is kept with the guide's records. No person has reviewed the result, so it is not marked Verified.
gaps: Whether the California Democratic Party supports Prop 40 (no source found)
Prop 40's own conflict clause is silent if a conflicting measure gets more votes; courts would decide

items.shortTitle: Special tax audits and spending limit
items.officialTitle: Prohibits new state taxes that exclude revenues from state spending limit. Requires audits for new state special taxes
items.plainEnglish: New state taxes enacted or taking effect on or after January 1, 2026 cannot be excluded from the state spending limit, or the state cannot collect them. The State Auditor reviews the programs a special tax proposed by citizen initiative would fund, while signatures are being gathered, and audits programs funded by new state special taxes every four years. If it gets more yes votes than another initiative on this ballot with a tax excluded from the spending limit, that whole measure is void.
items.why: Placed on the ballot by citizen petition (initiative). The official arguments below explain each side's stated goals.
items.yes: The State Auditor would review programs funded by proposed and approved special taxes, and the state might not be able to exclude new special tax spending from its spending limit.
items.no: The State Auditor's duties and the state spending limit requirements would not change.
items.benefits: New state taxes stay under the spending limit, and voters see audits of programs proposed special taxes would fund.
items.risks: If it gets more yes votes than Prop 40, LAO says courts could find a conflict and Prop 40 could be stopped. LAO also says the state might not be able to exclude new special tax spending from the spending limit, and calls the net fiscal effect unknown. Trade-off. More audits and spending-limit discipline, in exchange for less budget flexibility and the chance of blocking Prop 40.
items.affected: The State Auditor, future tax measures, and Prop 40.
items.fiscal: LAO estimates audit costs of low millions of dollars a year, growing over time. The overall budget effect is unknown.
items.evidence: Accountability. Pre-election audits are posted online, summarized in the voter guide, and must recommend ways to save at least 10% a year. Programs are audited again every four years. Nothing in the measure requires anyone to adopt the recommendations. Ratings on seven evidence factors, with reasons and sources, are in the full proposition tool.
items.uncertain: How much room is left under the spending limit.
items.argFor: Supporters' official argument says independent audits of programs funded by new special taxes bring transparency for taxpayers.
items.argAgainst: Opponents' official argument says it is billionaire-funded and designed to undo the Prop 40 billionaire tax.
items.supporters: CalCPAs, CalAsian Chamber of Commerce, California Taxpayers Association, former State Auditor Tom Hayes, former State Controller Steve Westly (official listing). CalMatters also lists Reform California. Backed by Building a Better California, which news reports say Sergey Brin funds heavily.
items.opponents: SEIU-UHW, Sen. Bernie Sanders (official listing). News reports add the California Democratic Party.
items.notes: Every field was audited on 2026-10-22 against the official voter guide, the LAO analysis, the official arguments and, where it could be read, the legal text, by automated research. A log of the corrections is kept with the guide's records. No person has reviewed the result, so it is not marked Verified.
gaps: Whether the four-year audits must include the 10% savings recommendation and be posted publicly like the pre-election audits

items.shortTitle: Ban on new asset and look-back taxes
items.officialTitle: Prohibits new state personal property taxes and certain retroactive state taxes
items.plainEnglish: Bans new state taxes on owning financial assets or other personal property, and new state taxes based on past conduct or past residency. The Legislature may pass a tax reaching back up to 365 days only during a declared disaster or fiscal emergency. Conflicting state taxes enacted on or after January 1, 2026 are void. If it gets more yes votes than a conflicting initiative on this ballot, that whole measure is void.
items.why: Placed on the ballot by citizen petition (initiative). The official arguments below explain each side's stated goals.
items.yes: The state could not establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
items.no: The state would continue to have the option to establish such taxes. No current tax changes either way.
items.benefits: A permanent ban on new state wealth-type and look-back taxes, which could also block Prop 40.
items.risks: If it gets more yes votes than Prop 40, LAO says courts could find a conflict and Prop 40 could be stopped. Undefined terms, such as ownership or control, may invite lawsuits. Trade-off. Certainty that owned assets will not face a new state tax, in exchange for giving up that revenue option and the chance of blocking Prop 40.
items.affected: Owners of financial assets and other personal property, and Prop 40.
items.fiscal: No dollar estimate. LAO says future tax revenue might not grow as much.
items.evidence: Accountability. No audit, reporting or outcome target. A self-executing ban enforced through the courts. Ratings on seven evidence factors, with reasons and sources, are in the full proposition tool.
items.uncertain: How courts will define a new tax, including changes to existing ones.
items.argFor: Supporters' official argument says it protects retirement and savings from new and retroactive taxes.
items.argAgainst: Opponents' official argument says it is billionaire-funded and designed to undo the Prop 40 billionaire tax.
items.supporters: California Professional Firefighters, State Building and Construction Trades Council, AMVETS Department of California, California Small Business Association, California Senior Alliance, Peace Officers Research Association of California (official listing, argument and rebuttal).
items.notes: Every field was audited on 2026-10-22 against the official voter guide, the LAO analysis, the official arguments and, where it could be read, the legal text, by automated research. A log of the corrections is kept with the guide's records. No person has reviewed the result, so it is not marked Verified.
gaps: Full official arguments not read word for word

items.shortTitle: Two-thirds vote for citizen local special taxes
items.officialTitle: Limits voters' ability to raise revenues for local government services
items.plainEnglish: From January 1, 2027, new, increased or extended local special taxes need two-thirds voter approval even when citizens put them on the ballot, the same bar as those placed by city councils and boards. General taxes are not covered. It also says no local government, including voters using the initiative, may impose ad valorem taxes on real property except as Article XIII D, Section 3(a)(1) of the state constitution allows. The official analysis does not discuss this clause. News reports say it came from a deal that kept a broader anti-tax initiative off the ballot.
items.why: Placed on the ballot by the California Legislature. The official arguments below explain each side's stated goals.
items.yes: Certain local government taxes would require two-thirds approval by voters. This covers citizen-proposed special taxes, including renewals.
items.no: Certain local government taxes could continue to be approved by voters with a majority vote.
items.benefits: From 2027, citizen-proposed local special taxes, including renewals, need two-thirds approval, so fewer may pass.
items.risks: Local services like fire and transit lose an easier funding path. Trade-off. One voting threshold for all local special taxes, in exchange for making citizen-led local funding harder to pass.
items.affected: Cities, counties, special districts, citizen tax campaigns.
items.fiscal: No dollar estimate. LAO says local revenue could be lower. CalMatters reports that Sonoma County's 2024 half-cent sales tax for wildfire and emergency services passed with 62%, below two-thirds.
items.evidence: Accountability. No reporting, audit or outcome target. The rule applies through election certification and the courts. Ratings on seven evidence factors, with reasons and sources, are in the full proposition tool.
items.uncertain: How much local revenue would be forgone, and how courts read its separate ban on citizen-initiative property taxes.
items.argFor: Supporters' official argument says court rulings opened a loophole and this restores Prop 13's two-thirds rule for special taxes.
items.argAgainst: Opponents' official argument and rebuttal say it cuts no taxes and lets just over one-third of voters block funding for fire, police, schools and roads.
items.supporters: California Taxpayers Association, Family Business Association of California, California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce, Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association.
items.opponents: California Professional Firefighters, California Federation of Teachers, Nurse Alliance of SEIU California, California School Employees Association (official listing and argument). News reports add the California Democratic Party.

items.officialTitle: Requires community health clinics spend 90% of revenue on program services
items.plainEnglish: Federally qualified health centers and similar clinics, with tribal clinics exempt, must spend at least 90% of revenue on program services. Any shortfall is paid as a penalty into escrow. It is returned only if the clinic reaches 90% within five years and agrees with the Department of Public Health on a plan to spend it on patient services. The department can grant one-year waivers. The Attorney General sets what counts, starting from IRS tax-form categories.
items.why: Placed on the ballot by citizen petition (initiative). The official arguments below explain each side's stated goals.
items.yes: Certain private nonprofit health care clinics would have to spend at least 90 percent of their revenue each year on providing health care services. LAO says clinics currently report about 80% on average.
items.no: The new requirement on health care clinic spending would not go into effect.
items.benefits: Clinics spend at least 90% of revenue on program services or pay the gap as a penalty, refundable if they comply within five years.
items.risks: LAO says some clinics that could not meet the requirement might close. Trade-off. Pressure to direct more clinic revenue to patient services, in exchange for penalties that could strain or close some clinics.
items.affected: Community health centers that served about 5.3 million patients in 2022, most with low incomes, according to their national association.
items.fiscal: A $50 million clinic at 80% would owe $5 million that year (this tool's example, using the 90% rule). LAO estimates state enforcement costs of low tens of millions of dollars a year, covered by fees on clinics.
items.evidence: Accountability. Yearly ratio filings posted by the Attorney General, audits, penalties, late-filing fines, patient lawsuits, and criminal penalties for knowingly false reports. Ratings on seven evidence factors, with reasons and sources, are in the full proposition tool.
items.uncertain: What the Attorney General will count as program services.
items.argFor: Supporters' official argument says some clinics spend under half their funding on patient care, and a 90% floor curbs executive spending.
items.argAgainst: Opponents' official argument calls it poorly drafted and says it would close many clinics serving millions of patients.
items.supporters: The official argument is signed by the initiative proponent and a community clinic worker. SEIU-UHW is the committee contact in the official guide and is named as the main proponent in news reports.
items.opponents: American Academy of Pediatrics California, California School Nurses Organization, California Medical Association (official argument). The official listing also names the California Academy of Family Physicians. News reports add the California Primary Care Association, Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California, and the Democratic and Republican parties.

items.officialTitle: Modifies environmental review for certain projects
items.plainEnglish: Nine project types (housing, water, clean energy, health facilities, fire and police stations, wildfire risk reduction, broadband, education facilities, transportation) can opt into a faster environmental review (CEQA) with firm deadlines. Lawsuits must be filed within 30 days and decided within 270 days including appeals. Courts may add up to 90 days, and longer only if all parties agree. Courts can pause only the flawed part of a project.
items.why: Placed on the ballot by citizen petition (initiative). The official arguments below explain each side's stated goals.
items.yes: Certain public and private projects would be eligible for new project review and court challenge procedures.
items.no: Public and private projects would continue to use existing project review and court challenge procedures.
items.benefits: Projects that opt in get environmental review and court decisions within fixed deadlines.
items.risks: Narrower review, including fewer alternatives considered and consultation only with federally recognized tribes. Trade-off. Faster, more predictable approvals, in exchange for narrower environmental and tribal review.
items.affected: Developers, public agencies, courts, tribes, neighbors of projects.
items.fiscal: LAO estimates initial state and local costs likely in the high tens of millions a year, possibly over $100 million, partly covered by fees. Long-term effects are uncertain.
items.evidence: Accountability. No reporting, audit or outcome target. Deadlines are enforced through the courts and applicant challenges when agencies miss them. Ratings on seven evidence factors, with reasons and sources, are in the full proposition tool.
items.uncertain: How many projects opt in and whether housing gets built faster. There is no neutral figure for how long CEQA lawsuits take today. A Holland & Knight report co-written by Jennifer Hernandez, who HousingWire reports helped write the measure, says CEQA trial and appellate proceedings typically take about five years.
items.argFor: Supporters' official argument says approvals are too slow and costly for housing, water, energy, schools and hospitals, and this keeps protections.
items.argAgainst: Opponents' official argument says it limits environmental review and public input while its funders profit.
items.supporters: California Children's Hospital Association, California Water Association, California Council on Affordable Housing (official listing and argument). News reports add the California Chamber of Commerce (sponsor), the California Hospital Association and the California Republican Party.
items.opponents: Coalition for Clean Air, Clean Water Action, California Environmental Voters (official argument). The official listing also names Physicians for Social Responsibility, Los Angeles and the National Wildlife Federation. News reports add the California Labor Federation, Sierra Club California and the California Democratic Party. The League of Women Voters of California opposes it in its own ballot recommendations.
